original_question: Let 2 < p < ∞ and let μ be a finite measure. Is the Banach space L^p(μ) Hilbert generated, meaning that some Hilbert space H admits a bounded linear operator T: H → L^p(μ) with dense range?
correct_elements: Your draft identifies the right target almost exactly: the paper’s official question is Problem 1.3, asking whether L^p(μ) is Hilbert generated for every finite measure μ and every exponent 2 < p < ∞. Your draft also correctly unpacks the meaning of “Hilbert generated” via the existence of a dense-range operator from a Hilbert space.
missing_details: The paper works throughout with real Banach spaces, so the intended Hilbert space H is real as well.
In the paper, an “operator” means a linear continuous map; your phrase “bounded linear operator” is equivalent, but this convention is part of the paper’s setup.
The density of the range is with respect to the norm topology on L^p(μ).
No separability, σ-finiteness, or other extra hypotheses are imposed on μ or on L^p(μ); the question is for an arbitrary finite measure.
The paper presents this as an open problem, not as a conjecture or theorem.
refined_question: Working over real Banach spaces, let 2 < p < ∞ and let μ be an arbitrary finite measure. Must the Banach space L^p(μ) be Hilbert generated; that is, does there exist a real Hilbert space H and a bounded linear operator T: H → L^p(μ) whose range is norm-dense in L^p(μ)?
justification: The nearest official formulation is exactly Problem 1.3 in Section 1.1. The paragraph immediately preceding it defines “Hilbert generated” and gives the relevant nearby context: L^p(μ) is Hilbert generated for 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, and for 2 < p < ∞ the problem is still open in general, although the paper notes positive cases when L^p(μ) is separable or has density character ω1. The only paper-faithful additions needed to make your draft fully stand-alone are the ambient real-scalar convention, the paper’s operator convention, and the fact that the dense range is norm-dense.
